B
A basis is defined by two conditions: its vectors must be linearly independent (no vector in the set can be written as a combination of the others) and they must span the space (any vector in the space can be formed by a combination of the basis vectors).

B
Changing the basis alters the coordinate system used to represent vectors and transformations, often to find a simpler representation (e.g., a diagonal matrix) that makes calculations easier or reveals underlying structures in the data.

B
A vector with coordinates (2, 0) in a basis means it has a length of 2 and is pointed entirely along the first basis vector. If this basis is rotated 45 degrees relative to the standard X-Y basis, the vector's coordinates in the standard basis would be (2*cos(45°), 2*sin(45°)), which is (√2, √2).

B
A change of basis matrix is multiplied by a vector's coordinates in one basis to find its coordinates in another basis.

B
To find a vector's coordinates in a new basis, you must find the scalar coefficients (the new coordinates) that allow the new basis vectors to sum up to the original vector. This is the definition of expressing a vector as a linear combination of a basis.
